intro: A hands-on introduction to humanoid robotics—from motors and actuators to coordinated motion and learned behavior. Over four weeks, students work in teams to assemble, program, and test components of an open-source humanoid.
introSecondary: Every student builds an actuator in Week 1 on the Berkeley Humanoid Lite platform. Teams then assemble, commission, and program the Metal2Humanoid, a larger custom humanoid, and the course ends with a public showcase of both robots on January 29.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: 12 integrated lecture-lab sessions of about three hours, tentatively Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays, plus supervised open lab time

facts.label: Enrollment
facts.value: 20 students in six teams of two to four; every student builds an actuator

facts.label: Prerequisites
facts.value: Basic programming, such as an introductory computer science or robotics course or equivalent experience. Assignments use Python. No prior hardware assembly, control theory, or machine learning experience is required.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: One primary robotics lab for all sessions, plus a larger venue for the final showcase

facts.label: Scheduled hours
facts.value: About 36 hours over 12 sessions, plus open lab time

facts.label: Final showcase
facts.value: Friday, January 29, 2027: public demonstrations of both humanoids with an invited audience

learn.text: BLDC motors, drivers, cycloidal gearboxes, encoders, and PID control. Every student assembles, calibrates, and tests their own actuator; by Friday, selected student-built actuators drive a prepared walking mechanism.

media.alt: Exploded render of the Berkeley Humanoid Lite 6512 cycloidal actuator: rear housing, dark motor shell, motor and input shafts, middle housing, output shaft halves, copper-colored cycloidal disk, and front housing laid out along the axis.
media.caption: Inside the actuator: an exploded render of the printed 6512 cycloidal module (BHL design, CC BY-SA 4.0).

learn.text: Kinematics, dynamics, balance, and humanoid architecture. Six teams assemble the Metal2Humanoid (legs, arms, torso, and integration), commission it, and run supported standing and walking tests, targeting walking by Friday.

media.alt: Render of a single Berkeley Humanoid Lite leg from hip actuators to flat foot.
media.caption: Teams assemble legs, arms, and torso in Week 2. A Berkeley Humanoid Lite leg is shown; the Metal2Humanoid design is being finalized (render, CC BY-SA 4.0).

learn.text: Reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and sim-to-real transfer. Teams train or fine-tune policies, develop one robot skill each, deploy feasible skills to hardware, and build a shared skill library.

media.alt: Four simulated humanoid robots walking on a checkered floor in a two-by-two grid.
media.caption: The Week 3 scaffold: the same training pipeline walking four open robots in MuJoCo, the starting point for team skills (simulation).

learn.text: Task planning and skill sequencing. Teams integrate skills into coordinated behaviors, rehearse, and present both humanoids at the public showcase on January 29.

media.alt: Front render of the complete Berkeley Humanoid Lite robot with legs, torso, and arms.
media.caption: Integration and showcase: both humanoids demonstrate skills and planning on January 29 (Berkeley Humanoid Lite render, CC BY-SA 4.0).

objectives: Individually assemble, calibrate, and test a functional actuator.
Demonstrate coordinated actuator control through a prepared Berkeley Humanoid Lite by the end of Week 1.
Assemble and commission the full Metal2Humanoid, targeting walking by the end of Week 2.
Develop and evaluate locomotion, manipulation, and other robot skills.
Integrate learned and programmed skills into coordinated robot behaviors.
Present the work at a public final showcase featuring both humanoid platforms.

format.title: How the course works
paragraphs: Four weeks is enough because the course is a guided tour of the whole stack, not a deep dive into any one field. Each session's lecture covers only the concepts needed for that session's hands-on work, hardware arrives as prepared kits with prefabricated parts and preflashed electronics, and software comes as fill-in-the-blank scaffolds with pretrained policies.

Each roughly three-hour session combines 20–40 minutes of lecture and demonstration, 90–120 minutes of guided hands-on work, and the remaining time for testing, debugging, and discussion. All sessions take place in the same lab, with additional open lab time for assembly, testing, and integration.

Students work in six teams of two to four. Every student completes an individual actuator; teams share responsibility for humanoid assembly, software development, and testing, and responsibilities may shift as the course progresses. Activities include four weekly assignments, lab participation, and the final showcase. No academic credit or formal grade is awarded.

outcomes.title: Outcomes and expectations
paragraphs: The course ends with a public showcase on January 29 featuring both humanoid platforms: student-built actuators, Berkeley Humanoid Lite walking and skills, the Metal2Humanoid walking and skills, and six team presentations with live or recorded demonstrations and lessons learned.

Milestones are targets, not promises. Assembling the full Metal2Humanoid and getting it walking by the end of Week 2 is ambitious; walking validation may extend into Week 3, and live demonstrations at the showcase depend on robot readiness and safety approval. Simulation and pretrained policies keep the software curriculum moving regardless of hardware delays, and every team prepares a recorded or simulated backup.
Builds are shared team builds. Each student keeps the experience of building and testing an actuator; the robots and kits stay with the course for future offerings and community builds.
